faqs.question: What are the main Halloween symbols and what do they mean?
faqs.answer: The core set is the ghost in a sheet (the friendly dead), the skeleton (death made playful), bats, owls and spiders (night and neglect), the witch with broom and cauldron (mischief and fortunes), the moon, apples and bonfires (charms and love fortunes), and the scarecrow and candy corn (harvest). Most of them were printed as Halloween decor between 1898 and 1921.

faqs.question: Are Halloween symbols really thousands of years old?
faqs.answer: Not as Halloween symbols. The earliest Halloween records we could open for 12 common symbols run from an 1898 party manual to a 1950s candy association. Apple games and autumn fires are older customs, but the claim that bats, owls or witches were Celtic Samhain emblems has no early document behind it.

faqs.question: Why is a Halloween ghost drawn as a white sheet?
faqs.answer: The sheet echoes the burial shroud: Shakespeare's Hamlet (c. 1600) already calls corpses "the sheeted dead". As a Halloween costume it is documented by 1898, when Martha Russell Orne's party manual has hosts greet guests covered with a sheet and hand out sheets so guests can play dead ancestors.

faqs.question: Why are bats a Halloween symbol?
faqs.answer: Bats were Halloween party decor long before vampire films. Orne's 1898 manual lists bats in shadow pantomimes and as souvenir shapes beside witches, cats and brooms. The popular story that bats gathered to eat insects at Celtic bonfires has no early source we could find.

faqs.question: Why do Halloween witches ride brooms and stir cauldrons?
faqs.answer: The cauldron comes straight from Shakespeare's Macbeth, where three witches chant "Fire, burn; and cauldron, bubble" in Act 4, Scene 1. Party books then made the figure comic: Orne lists broom-shaped souvenirs in 1898, and Guptill's 1915 book stages a witch stirring a large caldron of prize packages.

faqs.question: Why are owls and spiders linked to Halloween?
faqs.answer: Owls carried a death-omen reputation in general European folklore, and spiders suggest abandoned rooms. Their first Halloween appearance we found is Elizabeth Guptill's 1915 Complete Hallowe'en Book, which tells hosts to cut black cats, owls, bats and spiders from paper for the doorway.

faqs.question: Who invented candy corn, and was it made for Halloween?
faqs.answer: The usual story credits George Renninger of Philadelphia's Wunderle company, with Goelitz (now Jelly Belly) buying the recipe and selling it as "Chicken Feed". The Museum of the Grand Prairie says it had no Halloween association at first and dates the Halloween link to the 1950s. We found no dated primary record for the often-quoted 1888 invention date.

faqs.question: What does the moon mean on Halloween?
faqs.answer: In old Halloween charms the moon set the hour: Orne's 1898 manual tells readers to walk backward in the moonlight holding a mirror to glimpse a future partner. A Middlebury College card dated 20 October 1909 is catalogued as a "Moon head" Halloween card, so the face-in-the-moon look was on cards by then.

faqs.question: Why did Halloween postcards matter so much to the symbols?
faqs.answer: A 2024 study in The Journal of American Culture dates the golden age of Halloween postcards to about 1900 to 1920. A postcard cost 1 cent to buy and 1 cent to mail, US sales passed one billion cards by 1909, and that volume repeated the same small set of figures until they became the holiday's look.

faqs.question: Can I send Halloween symbols to one person as a card?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you want a greeting rather than decor. SubhSandesh's interactive Halloween card lets you choose the costume on their Boo License, including ghost, witch, skeleton, black cat or bat, and the premium page adds a voice note up to 60 seconds and up to 12 photos. Both are one-person pages, not party invitations.

faqs.question: When is Halloween in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Halloween is always 31 October. It falls on a Saturday in 2026 and a Sunday in 2027, with All Saints' Day on 1 November each year.

# Halloween Symbols and Meanings: Where Each Icon Really Came From

Halloween symbols and meanings mostly date from American party books and penny postcards of 1898 to 1920, not from ancient Celts. Ghosts in sheets, bats, owls, spiders, brooms and cauldrons are all printed as Halloween decor by 1915, and the "ancient" stories attached to them usually have no document behind them. The postcard that fixed this picture was a 1-cent card anyone could read; its successor is a link, and 48.3% of SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, with each page viewed 11.1 times on average. Below: 12 symbols, the earliest dated Halloween record we could open for each, and the myth worth dropping. Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027.

## What turns an image into a Halloween symbol?

A Halloween symbol is an image people recognise as meaning "31 October" without a caption. Most earned that status through repetition in print: party manuals told hosts what to cut out, and postcard publishers sold the same figures by the million.

A 2024 peer-reviewed analysis of [golden-age Halloween postcards by Adrienne Darrah in The Journal of American Culture](https://doi.org/10.1111/jacc.13580) dates the boom to roughly 1900–1920. It records a May 1898 law letting private postcards travel at the same 1-cent rate as government ones, US sales passing one billion cards by 1909, and the decline beginning around 1910.

## 12 Halloween symbols, each with its earliest dated record

Each entry gives what it means today, the earliest Halloween record we opened, and the myth to drop. The jack-o'-lantern and the black cat are left to their own guides; the short version is that the carved lantern is documented, while most black-cat lore is general superstition rather than Halloween-specific.

### 1. Ghost in a white sheet

Today it means a friendly dead visitor. In [Martha Russell Orne's 1898 party manual](https://archive.org/details/orne-a), hosts greet guests "covered with a sheet" and hand guests sheets of their own to play dead ancestors. The sheet is older than the party: Shakespeare's Hamlet (c. 1600) has "the sheeted dead" walking Rome, meaning corpses in burial shrouds. Myth to drop: that Celts set extra dinner places for ghosts on Samhain. We found no early source saying so.

### 2. Skeleton

It stands for death made playful. In [Elizabeth Guptill's Complete Hallowe'en Book (1915)](https://archive.org/details/completehallowee00gupt), a ghost-party invitation shows a draped figure with "a long, skeleton arm" beckoning, and a play costume is black with a skeleton painted in white. The medieval memento mori skeleton is real, but it belonged to sermons and church walls, not to any 31 October custom. Myth to drop: that skeletons were a Samhain emblem.

### 3. Bat

It now signals night and the spooky-cute. Orne's 1898 manual lists bats twice: in shadow pantomimes "representing witches, fairies, gnomes, cats, ghosts, bats" and as pen-wiper prizes shaped like "witches, cats, bats, brooms". Myth to drop: that bats gathered at Celtic bonfires to eat insects and so became the night's mascot. It is a tidy story with no early text behind it.

### 4. Owl

It means wisdom by day and a death omen by night. Its first Halloween appearance we found is Guptill 1915, where "black cats, owls, bats and spiders may be cut from paper" for a doorway, and a fortune-teller's potion holds "the eyes of an owl". The owl-as-omen belief is general European folklore, not a Halloween invention. Myth to drop: that owls swooped down to eat the souls of the dying on this one night.

### 5. Spider and web

It means neglect: the room nobody has entered for years. The spider joins the paper-cutting list in Guptill 1915, alongside owls and bats. Webs strung across doorways as decor are harder to date: neither Orne nor Guptill mentions a cobweb. Myth to drop: that a spider seen on Halloween carries a dead relative's spirit. We could not trace it to any print source.

### 6. Witch and broom

The witch means mischief more than menace now. Orne 1898 already pairs "witches, cats, bats, brooms" as souvenir shapes, and Guptill 1915 places a witch doll "with a tiny black cat and a broom" guarding the fortune cake. Myth to drop: that the Halloween witch preserves a Celtic priestess. The figure comes from older European witch imagery that party books made comic.

### 7. Cauldron

It means a brew of fortunes, then a punch bowl. The literary source is easy to pin: the three witches in [Shakespeare's Macbeth (Act 4, Scene 1)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1533) chant "Fire, burn; and cauldron, bubble" over a pot that includes "wool of bat". Guptill 1915 borrows it directly, with a costumed witch stirring a "large caldron" of sawdust and prize packages. Myth to drop: that a Celtic cauldron of rebirth explains the decoration.

### 8. Moon

It means the hour for charms to work. Orne 1898 tells readers to walk backward "in the moonlight with a mirror" to see a future partner. Middlebury College holds a Halloween card catalogued as ["Moon head", dated 20 October 1909](https://archive.org/details/c132_halloween_card_moon_head), and Guptill 1915 has a cardboard "Man in the Moon" that rises and winks. Myth to drop: that every historic Halloween had a full moon. The phase changes each year.

### 9. Apple

It means love fortunes. Apples appear 13 times in Orne's 1898 manual, including apples heaped among the autumn-leaf decorations and silk apple-shaped prizes. The games themselves are older and are covered in histories of Halloween customs. Myth to drop: the apple as a Roman Pomona survival. We found no ancient source tying Pomona to 31 October.

### 10. Bonfire

It means protection. By 1898 Orne was already explaining the "Hallowe'en fire" as "a charm against evil spirits" and describing seventeenth-century farmers circling their fields with a lighted torch, with no source given for either. That shows how early the protective reading became stock copy, repeated rather than checked. Myth to drop: that every Halloween fire was lit to keep the dead away.

### 11. Scarecrow

It means harvest, and it came late. Neither Orne 1898 nor Guptill 1915 uses it as Halloween decor. A 1921 Thomas Nelson one-act play titled The Scarecrow: A Halloween Fantasy is the earliest Halloween pairing in the archive listings we searched. Myth to drop: that scarecrows guarded Samhain fields from spirits. It is an autumn farm image adopted by the holiday.

### 12. Candy corn

It means "Halloween sweets" in North America. A 2023 note from the [Museum of the Grand Prairie](https://www.museumofthegrandprairie.org/Explore/Blog/the-history-of-candy-corn) says Goelitz bought the recipe from Philadelphia's Wunderle company, credits George Renninger, and sold it as "Chicken Feed" to farm families with "no association to Halloween whatsoever". It dates the Halloween link to the 1950s. Myth to drop: a precise 1888 invention date. We found it only in secondary retellings, not in a dated primary record.

## Halloween symbols compared: oldest record, source and myth

The table groups the 12 symbols into five families. Dates are the earliest Halloween record we could open, not the age of the image itself.

| Symbol group | Earliest Halloween record we opened | Source type | Myth with no early document |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ghost in sheet, skeleton | 1898 (sheet), 1915 (skeleton) | US party manuals | Celts set places for the dead |
| Bat, owl, spider | 1898 (bat), 1915 (owl, spider) | US party manuals | Bonfire insects drew bats and owls |
| Witch, broom, cauldron | 1898 (broom), 1915 (cauldron) | Party manuals; Macbeth c. 1606 | Celtic priestess or rebirth cauldron |
| Moon, apple, bonfire | 1898 (all three) | Orne 1898; Middlebury card 1909 | Every old Halloween had a full moon |
| Scarecrow, candy corn | 1921 (scarecrow), 1950s (candy corn) | Play title; museum note 2023 | Candy corn made for Halloween in 1888 |

The pattern: every Halloween record we opened falls between 1898 and the 1950s. Apple games and autumn fires are older customs, but their use as printed Halloween symbols starts with the party-book era.

## Why 1898–1920 fixed the Halloween picture

The same few figures repeat because they were cheap to print and easy to cut. Darrah's study notes a postcard cost 1 cent to buy and 1 cent to mail, against 3 cents for a sealed greeting card. Because the message rode on the open back, every card advertised the sender's taste to the postman and the household.

Party manuals did the rest. Orne in 1898 and Guptill in 1915 give overlapping cut-out lists of cats, bats and brooms, which suggests a shared commercial vocabulary rather than inherited folklore. Darrah reports that the 1909 Payne-Aldrich tariff priced out German-printed cards, and the boom faded from 1910. By then the kit was set.

## Sending the symbols to one person

The [interactive Halloween card with a Boo License](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) lets you pick the costume printed on their licence: ghost, witch, vampire, pumpkin, black cat, skeleton, mummy or bat. That covers four of the 12 symbols above, and the card takes about five minutes with up to six photos. Both pages offer an optional password, which 38.5% of SubhSandesh creators set before sharing.

If you want more room, the [cinematic Halloween page with a voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice message up to 60 seconds, up to 12 photos, a bat that delivers your letter and a moon that turns into a heart. It takes about ten minutes. For a different occasion later, you can [browse every SubhSandesh template](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

## When a symbol list, or our page, is the wrong tool

Both pages are one-person greeting pages, not party decorations or invitations for a crowd. For a classroom, office or porch, the 1915 approach still wins: paper bats, owls and spiders take an afternoon with scissors and everyone sees them at once.

The page also assumes a screen. 48.3% of our pages are opened on a phone and 51.6% of views come from non-touch screens such as laptops, so a recipient who rarely uses either is better served by a handwritten card. The interface is English only, and neither page explains folklore: the history lives here, and the card is just the greeting.
